stages.source_description: Part 1: Introduction (Slides 1-3: Hook, SDG 1 definition, Taiwan context with critical setup)

title.zh: 看見身邊隱形貧窮

A2.text: Good morning. Poverty is not always far away. Look around: a classmate skips lunch, a family works long hours, a student has no quiet place to study.
A2.workbook_text: Good morning. Before we talk about poverty far away, let us look around us. Poverty can be hidden in a classmate who skips lunch, a family working long hours, or a student without a quiet place to study.

A1.text: Hello everyone. Poverty is not always far away. Some classmates may skip lunch or have no quiet place to study. Today, we talk about SDG 1.

B1.text: SDG 1 opens with an uncomfortable question. Can real poverty survive inside a developed society like Taiwan? It can, and it quietly decides how far a young person in this room is able to go.
B1.workbook_text: Good morning, everyone. SDG 1 begins with one uncomfortable question: can poverty exist in a developed place like Taiwan? The answer is yes. It may be hidden, but it still shapes students' lives and futures.

B2.text: Prosperity is remarkably good at hiding hardship, which is why my first question is uncomfortable. Does poverty still exist in a developed Taiwan, or have we been conditioned not to notice it?

title.zh: 消除各種形式的貧窮

A2.text: Goal one asks every country to end poverty in all its forms. That is not only about income. It is health care, housing, education, and a fair chance to start again.
A2.workbook_text: SDG 1 means ending poverty in all its forms. It is not only about income. It is also about safety, health care, education, housing, and the chance to recover when life becomes difficult.

A1.text: SDG 1 means no poverty. People need enough money, food, a safe home, health care, and a chance to learn.

B1.text: SDG 1 asks governments to end poverty in every form. That includes low income, unsafe housing and weak social protection. The goal treats poverty as a fault in the system, not a personal failure.
B1.workbook_text: SDG 1 asks countries to end poverty in every form. This includes low income, unsafe housing, weak social protection, and limited access to services. It reminds us that poverty is a system problem, not only a personal failure.

B2.text: Ending poverty in all of its forms is the first global goal, and that wording deliberately reaches past household income. It covers housing, protection and access, so poverty is framed as a structural condition rather than a personal fault.

title.zh: 貧窮不只是收入問題

A2.text: Look at Taiwan. We have good schools and new technology, but not every family feels safe. Some struggle with rent, some with medical bills, some with jobs that never last.
A2.workbook_text: In Taiwan, many students have good schools and technology. However, not every family has the same support. Some families struggle with rent, care work, medical costs, or unstable jobs. This is why SDG 1 still matters here.

A1.text: Taiwan has many schools and technology, but some families still have a hard life. Rent, work, and health costs can be heavy.

B1.text: Taiwan has strong education, health care and technology. Even so, inequality remains. A family can look normal from outside while carrying debt, nursing a sick parent, or living on work that could end tomorrow.
B1.workbook_text: Taiwan has strong education, health care, and technology, but inequality still exists. A family can look normal from outside while facing debt, care pressure, or unstable work. SDG 1 helps us notice these hidden struggles.

B2.text: Taiwan has excellent schools, health care for everyone and world-class technology, and yet inequality here has proved stubborn. A household can look completely normal while carrying debt, nursing a sick relative, or living on work that could vanish tomorrow.

stages.source_description: Part 2: Problem Identification (Slides 4-6: Key challenges, evidence, and critical questions)
stages.language_pattern: present progressive for trends / this causes ...

title.zh: 工作貧窮與不穩定就業

A2.text: The first problem is working poverty. People work hard and still feel unsafe. Short contracts, low pay and long hours break their plans, and tired parents lose time with their children.
A2.workbook_text: The first challenge is working poverty. Some people work hard but still cannot feel secure. Temporary jobs, low wages, and long hours make planning difficult. If parents are stressed, children's learning can also be affected.

A1.text: Some people work hard but still do not have enough money. Unstable jobs make family life and school life harder.

B1.text: Working poverty matters because hard work no longer brings security. Parents on temporary contracts lose the hours and the energy their children need. Poverty then travels into the next generation, and that is how it repeats.
B1.workbook_text: Working poverty is a serious problem because effort does not always lead to security. When parents face temporary contracts or low pay, they may have less time and energy to support their children. Poverty can then pass across generations.

B2.text: Working poverty unsettles us because it breaks the promise that effort brings security. Parents trapped in temporary contracts give up the attention their children need, and the disadvantage is passed on, quietly, to the next generation.

title.zh: 居住成本加重家庭壓力

A2.text: Rent is the next weight. When it is high, families spend less on food, books and tutoring. Some students move house often or share one crowded room, where study is hard.
A2.workbook_text: Housing is another pressure. When rent is high, families may spend less on food, books, tutoring, or transportation. Students might move often or live in crowded rooms. A stable home is part of learning.

A1.text: High rent can hurt families. They may have less money for food, books, or buses. A safe home helps students learn.

B1.text: Housing costs create poverty quietly. Once the rent takes too much of the income, everything else has to be sacrificed. Students who move often or share a crowded room lose sleep, concentration and confidence.
B1.workbook_text: Housing costs can quietly create poverty. If too much income goes to rent, families must cut other needs. For students, crowded housing or frequent moving can reduce sleep, concentration, and confidence at school.

B2.text: What housing quietly does is eliminate everything else a family might have bought, because an unaffordable rent comes out first. Students who move house often or share a crowded room lose sleep, concentration and the confidence that classrooms reward.

title.zh: 數位落差限制機會

A2.text: Poverty also shows up online. Some students have fast internet, a laptop and parents who can help. Others share one phone, so a digital gap slowly turns into a learning gap.
A2.workbook_text: Poverty also appears online. Some students have fast internet, laptops, and parents who can help. Others share one phone or cannot join online learning easily. Digital gaps become learning gaps.

A1.text: Some students have computers and good internet. Some only have a phone. This makes learning unfair.

B1.text: Digital access is now part of basic opportunity. Without a reliable device, a good connection and someone to ask, a student cannot fully join homework, research or AI learning. Their poverty is simply harder to see.
B1.workbook_text: Digital access is now part of basic opportunity. Without a reliable device, internet connection, and support, students cannot fully join homework, research, or AI learning. Poverty becomes less visible, but more powerful.

B2.text: Digital participation has become a precondition for opportunity rather than a convenience. A student without a working device, a stable connection and help at home is shut out of homework, research and artificial intelligence.

stages.source_description: Part 3: Achievements and Progress (Slides 7-9: What Taiwan has done well, with scrutiny)

title.zh: 社會安全網守住基本生活

A2.text: Taiwan has safety nets: social help, health insurance, and local offices. They protect basic needs. But does that help reach us before a small problem turns into a crisis?
A2.workbook_text: Taiwan has important safety nets, such as social assistance, health insurance, emergency help, and local services. These systems protect basic needs. Still, the hardest question is whether support reaches people before problems become crises.

A1.text: Taiwan has help for poor families, health care, and emergency support. These programs protect people, but they must reach people early.

B1.text: Taiwan has built several safety nets: health insurance, social welfare, emergency relief and local service centers. These protect many people. However, good policy must be easy to find, simple to apply for and respectful to use.
B1.workbook_text: Taiwan has built several safety nets, including health insurance, social welfare, emergency relief, and local service centers. These protect many people. However, good policy must be easy to find, simple to apply for, and respectful to use.

B2.text: Taiwan's protective net is genuinely broad: National Health Insurance, social welfare, emergency relief and local service centers. Only when help is easy to find will it reach the household that needs it before the crisis arrives.

title.zh: 校園支持與營養照顧

A2.text: Schools can soften the blow. Free meals, counseling, scholarships and after-school classes all help. A teacher who notices one quiet child early can change that child's whole year.
A2.workbook_text: Schools can reduce poverty's effect on children. Meal programs, scholarships, counseling, after-school support, and teachers who notice students early are all important. School is not only a classroom. It can be a support system.

A1.text: Schools can help children. Free meals, scholarships, teachers, and after-school help make students feel safe and ready to learn.

B1.text: Schools are strong because they see students every day. Meal support, scholarships, counseling and after-school clubs take real weight off a family. A teacher who notices early becomes a bridge to local services.
B1.workbook_text: Schools are powerful because they see students every day. Meal support, scholarships, counseling, and after-school programs can reduce pressure on families. When teachers notice needs early, school becomes a bridge between students and community resources.

B2.text: Schools matter enormously because they see students every single day, which no welfare office could manage. Free meals, scholarships, counseling and supervised study take real weight off a household, and an alert teacher becomes the bridge to community help.

title.zh: 社區組織補足服務缺口

A2.text: Community groups help too. Food banks, social workers, religious groups and NGOs find people that big systems miss. Gifts alone are not enough, because real support builds skills and dignity.
A2.workbook_text: Community groups also help. Food banks, social workers, religious groups, NGOs, and volunteer teams can find needs that official systems miss. But charity alone is not enough. Long-term support must build skills and dignity.

A1.text: Community groups can give food, care, and help. But help should not only be gifts. It should build confidence and skills.

B1.text: Local organizations often understand a neighborhood better than any ministry does. They provide food, tutoring, care and job news. Yet SDG 1 is not charity, because the goal is to give people choices, skills and dignity.
B1.workbook_text: Community organizations often understand local problems deeply. They may provide food, tutoring, care, or job information. Yet SDG 1 is not just charity. The goal is to help people gain choices, skills, and dignity.

B2.text: Civil society reaches the households that the official system overlooks, providing food, tutoring, daily care and job information. SDG 1, however, is not an argument for charity, because the aim is capability and dignity rather than dependence.

stages.source_description: Part 4: Solutions and Youth Action (Slides 10-12: Practical solutions and local innovation)

title.zh: 理財素養培養韌性

A2.text: So what can we do? One answer is financial literacy. Students can plan a budget, save a little, borrow with care, and learn how to spot a scam.
A2.workbook_text: One solution is financial literacy. Students can learn budgeting, saving, responsible borrowing, and how to avoid scams. These skills do not solve poverty alone, but they help young people make safer choices in the future.

A1.text: Students can learn how to budget, save, and avoid scams. Money skills help us make safer choices.

B1.text: Financial literacy gives you real power in daily life. Knowing about budgets, savings, debt, insurance and scams leads to better choices. Of course school cannot replace a fair wage, but it does build personal resilience.
B1.workbook_text: Financial literacy gives students practical power. By learning budgets, savings, debt, insurance, and scams, young people can make better decisions. Of course, education cannot replace fair wages, but it can strengthen personal resilience.

B2.text: Financial literacy offers a modest but real form of personal power, covering budgets, savings, debt, insurance and the recognition of fraud. It cannot substitute for a decent wage, though it does tend to strengthen resilience against a sudden shock.

title.zh: 數據地圖看見隱性需求

A2.text: Data can help as well. Students can map what is missing near them: food, buses, care for old people, classes after school. But data should guide our kindness, not replace it.
A2.workbook_text: Technology can also help. Students can use simple data maps to understand where help is needed: food access, public transportation, elderly care, or after-school programs. Data should guide kindness, not replace it.

A1.text: Technology can help us see needs. Students can make maps about food, buses, care, or learning support.

B1.text: Data tools can reveal the poverty that nobody has counted. Students can map service locations, transport gaps or after-school resources, and a community then chooses more wisely. But every data point is still a real person.
B1.workbook_text: Data tools can reveal hidden poverty. For example, students can map service locations, transportation gaps, or after-school resources. Used carefully, data helps communities make smarter decisions. But every data point is still a real person.

B2.text: Careful analysis can expose the hardship that an average hides, letting students map where services, transport and after-school help run out. Communities can then aim their money well, provided we remember that each data point is a real person.

title.zh: 服務學習連結真實行動

A2.text: Service learning turns ideas into action. We can visit a local group, write posters in two languages, or teach younger children. We learn most when we work beside people.
A2.workbook_text: Service learning connects English, SDGs, and action. Students can interview local groups, write bilingual posters, design donation guides, or teach younger students. The best learning is not only speaking about problems, but working with people.

A1.text: Students can help local groups, make English posters, or teach younger children. We learn by doing.

B1.text: Service learning turns SDG 1 into real experience. Students can interview social workers, build bilingual guides or help with tutoring. Their English gets better as well, because they speak for a purpose, not for a grade.
B1.workbook_text: Service learning turns SDG 1 into real experience. Students can interview social workers, create bilingual resources, or support tutoring programs. This also improves English because students speak for a real purpose, not only for a grade.

B2.text: Service learning turns an abstract target into something actually done: interviews with social workers, guides written in two languages, hours in a tutoring program. English tends to improve under those conditions, because the language finally serves a real purpose.

stages.source_description: Part 5: Implications and Future Challenges (Slides 13-16: Broader impacts and debates)

title.zh: 高齡社會提高貧窮風險

A2.text: Taiwan is growing older fast. Many old people live alone and need care, money, transport, and help with their phone. Poverty follows health and family, not only pay.
A2.workbook_text: Future poverty may grow with aging. Older people living alone may need care, money, transport, and digital support. Young people should understand that poverty is connected to health, family structure, and public services.

A1.text: Taiwan has more older people. Some live alone and need money, care, buses, and digital help.

B1.text: An aging society changes the shape of poverty. Older adults may live alone, manage illness, or struggle with services that have moved online. SDG 1 therefore connects welfare, transport, health care and community, not just income.
B1.workbook_text: An aging society changes poverty. Some older adults may live alone, have health problems, or struggle with digital services. SDG 1 therefore connects welfare, transportation, health care, and community relationships, not just income.

B2.text: An aging society is shifting poverty towards older citizens, especially those who live alone, manage illness, or give up on services that have moved online. SDG 1 therefore connects welfare, transport, health care and the strength of local relationships.

title.zh: 移民家庭需要公平資源

A2.text: Migrant workers and new immigrant families need a fair door in. Language, forms and customs make help hard to reach. When a service is clear, the whole family can use it.
A2.workbook_text: Another challenge is fair access for migrant workers and new immigrant families. Language, documents, and cultural differences can make services hard to use. Inclusive support helps children and adults participate fully in society.

A1.text: Migrant workers and new immigrant families may face language problems. Fair support helps them live and learn.

B1.text: Poverty is harder to escape for migrant workers and new immigrant families. Language and paperwork can build a wall around help. If the message is clear and multilingual, more people will ask for it.
B1.workbook_text: Poverty can be harder for migrant workers and new immigrant families because language and paperwork create barriers. If services are confusing, people may not receive help. Inclusion means making information clear, multilingual, and respectful.

B2.text: For migrant workers and new immigrant families, entitlement and access are split by language, paperwork and official habit. Help that cannot be understood is help that does not exist, so inclusion has to be clear, multilingual and respectful.

title.zh: 氣候衝擊傷害弱勢群體

A2.text: Climate disasters make poverty worse. Floods and heat hit poor homes hardest, because they have less money saved and fewer ways out. Climate action is part of this fight.
A2.workbook_text: Climate disasters can also deepen poverty. Floods, heat, and extreme weather hurt low-income families first because they have fewer savings and fewer choices. SDG 1 is connected to climate action and disaster preparation.

A1.text: Floods and hot weather hurt poor families more. They have less money to recover. Climate action also fights poverty.

B1.text: Climate risk is a poverty issue. When a disaster arrives, low-income families lose more and recover far more slowly. So shelters, insurance, clear warnings and neighbors who check on each other have to be ready first.
B1.workbook_text: Climate risk is a poverty issue. When disasters happen, low-income families often lose more and recover more slowly. Preparing shelters, insurance, public information, and community networks can protect vulnerable people before emergencies arrive.

B2.text: Climate change acts as an inequality multiplier, because the same flood hits two homes very differently, depending on savings and insurance. Adaptation is poverty policy, and shelters, advice and local networks must exist before the emergency arrives.

title.zh: 用尊嚴改變援助方式

A2.text: Now, dignity. Help should never make a person feel small. If we only see weakness, we miss the strength that is already there, so we should listen first.
A2.workbook_text: Finally, we must talk about dignity. Helping people should not make them feel ashamed. If we only see poor people as weak, we miss their strengths. Real support listens, respects, and works together.

A1.text: People need help with respect. Poverty is not shame. We should listen and work together.

B1.text: Dignity changes the way support is given. Poverty should never be treated as shame or laziness, because many people are strong and simply face unfair conditions. Respectful help asks people what they actually need.
B1.workbook_text: Dignity changes the way we help. Poverty should not be treated as shame or laziness. Many people are strong but face unfair conditions. Respectful support asks people what they need and includes them in decisions.

B2.text: Dignity deserves treatment as a design principle rather than a courtesy, since help delivered with contempt is often refused. People in poverty are disadvantaged rather than lacking, and support built with them works better than support built for them.

stages.source_description: Part 6: Conclusion and Call to Action (Slides 17-20: Summary, strong end, student action)

title.zh: SDG1 代表共享安全感

A2.text: To sum up, this goal is about shared safety. Poverty touches housing, health, education and dreams. Taiwan already helps, but help must come sooner and reach further.
A2.workbook_text: To sum up, SDG 1 is about shared security. Poverty affects education, health, housing, and dreams. Taiwan has support systems, but we still need earlier help, better access, and stronger community action.

A1.text: SDG 1 is about safety for everyone. Poverty affects school, health, homes, and dreams. We need better support.

B1.text: In summary, SDG 1 is not only about money. It is about whether everyone can live with safety and opportunity. Taiwan has clearly progressed, yet hidden poverty still asks us to improve access, timing and fairness.
B1.workbook_text: In summary, SDG 1 is not only about money. It is about whether everyone can live with safety and opportunity. Taiwan has made progress, but hidden poverty still asks us to improve access, timing, and fairness.

B2.text: The overall position is encouraging without being anything like sufficient, because the institutions exist and the coverage is broad. What is still missing is access, timing and the fairness with which help actually reaches the households that need it.

title.zh: 挑戰責怪與刻板印象

A2.text: We also need to drop the blame. Low pay, high prices, illness, family care, a flood: these push people down. Blaming is easy, but understanding is useful.
A2.workbook_text: We also need to challenge stereotypes. It is easy to blame poor people, but poverty is often caused by low wages, high costs, illness, care duties, or disasters. Understanding the system helps us respond wisely.

A1.text: We should not blame poor people. Many problems come from low pay, illness, high costs, or family care.

B1.text: The most useful change may be our own language. Calling people lazy ends the conversation at once. Asking which barriers they meet opens it, because we then have to discuss wages, rent, health, transport and education.
B1.workbook_text: A key step is changing our language. If we say poor people are lazy, we stop thinking. If we ask what barriers they face, we can discuss wages, rent, health, transport, and education more honestly.

B2.text: Perhaps the most powerful reform available to us is vocabulary, because calling people lazy ends the analysis at once. Asking instead which obstacles they meet forces a serious conversation about wages, rent, health care, transport and education.

title.zh: 建立技能、連結與發聲能力

A2.text: You are young, but you can start now. Learn English and share these ideas, use data to show the problem, join a group near you. Together, small actions become powerful.
A2.workbook_text: Young people can help by building skills, networks, and voice. We can learn English to share SDG ideas, use data to explain problems, and join local projects. Small actions become powerful when they are organized.

A1.text: Young people can learn English, use data, and join local projects. Small actions can become strong together.

B1.text: Students are not too young to act on this. They can run bilingual campaigns, volunteer, collect stories, design simple tools, or present their ideas to the school. PechaKucha turns private study into a public voice.
B1.workbook_text: Students are not too young to act. They can create bilingual campaigns, volunteer, collect stories, design simple tools, or present ideas to the school. PechaKucha is one way to turn learning into a public voice.

B2.text: Students often underestimate their own power: bilingual campaigns, volunteer work, stories, simple tools, a talk given in front of a real audience. PechaKucha turns private study into public argument, which is exactly what a democracy needs.

title.zh: 從在地行動開始消除貧窮

A2.text: So let's start where we stand. See poverty clearly, speak with respect, and act in our own school and community. A fair future begins with what we choose to notice today.
A2.workbook_text: Thank you for listening. SDG 1 asks us to see poverty clearly and act with respect. Let us start from our school, our community, and our words. A fair future begins with what we choose to notice today.

A1.text: Thank you for listening. Let us see poverty, respect people, and help in our school and community. We can start today.

B1.text: Ending poverty sounds enormous, yet the action usually starts nearby. Notice a need, check the facts, speak respectfully and work with somebody else. If we connect English, the SDGs and action, students can become real changemakers.
B1.workbook_text: Thank you. Ending poverty sounds huge, but action can begin nearby: notice a need, learn the facts, speak respectfully, and work with others. If we connect English, SDGs, and action, students can become real changemakers.

B2.text: Eliminating poverty sounds impossibly large, yet every credible version begins locally, by noticing a need, checking the facts, speaking with respect and working with other people. A fair future begins with whatever this generation decides is worth noticing today.
